s: Henry VIII's gun fort turned prime ministers' retreat
w: Built in 1539 as one of Henry VIII's three Channel forts, its four bastions and moated keep once held 39 guns trained on the Downs anchorage. When invasion never came, Walmer became home to the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports - a post filled by Pitt and Wellington, who turned the fortress into a garden retreat.
_facts: Built 1539-40 under Henry VIII's King's Device coastal defence programme
Moated stone castle with keep and four bastions, 39 firing positions
Became official residence of the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports in the 18th century
Wardens included William Pitt, the Duke of Wellington and Lord Granville, who added gardens

s: A ruined moated castle staged inside its own garden
w: The ruins of a medieval moated manor sit on a lake island, kept as a picturesque folly once a new house rose on the hill above in 1835-43. Anthony Salvin's Tudor Revival mansion looks over slopes thick with rhododendron and wisteria. It opened to the public only in 2007, the year after its last resident died.
_facts: Medieval moated manor ruin (Scotney Old Castle) sits on an island in a small lake
Gardens are a Site of Special Scientific Interest in the picturesque style
New house (Scotney New Castle) built 1835-1843 by Anthony Salvin in Tudor Revival style
Opened to the public in 2007 after resident Elizabeth Hussey died in 2006

s: A rebel's castle, seized, ruined, and rebuilt by hand
w: Thrown up without permission during The Anarchy, torn down, then rebuilt legally with one of England's first long galleries. The Crown seized it in 1554 after Thomas Wyatt the Younger's rebellion against Mary failed, and decay did the rest until Sir Martin Conway rescued it in the 1900s. Now a wedding venue.
_facts: First fortification built without permission during The Anarchy (1135-53)
Refortified with royal permission in the 13th century, gained one of England's first long galleries
Seized by the Crown in 1554 after Sir Thomas Wyatt the Younger's failed rebellion
Restored by Sir Martin Conway in the early 20th century; later home to Carmelite friars, now private

s: The Roman harbour buried beneath modern Dover
w: Before Dover was Dover, this was Dubris - Rome's closest crossing point to the continent, and one of two starting points of Watling Street alongside Richborough. The Dour that gave the harbour its water now runs underground through the town. Garrisoned first by the Classis Britannica fleet, later by Saxon Shore troops.
_facts: Roman port also known as Portus Dubris, on the site of modern Dover
One of two starting points of Watling Street, alongside Rutupiae (Richborough)
Fortified and garrisoned first by the Classis Britannica, later by Saxon Shore Fort troops
The River Dour, which gave the harbour its water, is now covered for much of its course

s: A Grade I Palladian house with barely a paper trail
w: A Grade I listed Palladian country house standing quietly in the village of Mereworth - one of Kent's most architecturally serious houses, and one of its least documented, tucked well away from the tourist trail.
_facts: Grade I listed Palladian country house in Mereworth, Kent

s: Roman road, Pilgrims' trail, and a buried Neolithic house
w: A chalk scarp on the North Downs where a Roman road climbs past the ancient Pilgrims' Way, quarried for chalk across two centuries, now a nature reserve. High Speed 1 tunnels beneath it, and the dig turned up a Neolithic long house. Walkers cross its top past Kit's Coty, with only the Lower Bell pub left standing.
_facts: Chalk hill on the North Downs, quarried for chalk in the 18th-19th centuries
Prehistoric Pilgrims' Way trackway runs along its foot, North Downs Way along its top
High Speed 1 tunnels beneath the hill; archaeology ahead of it found a Neolithic long house
Upper Bell pub closed 2005 and was demolished 2013, leaving the Lower Bell

s: Where Becket was murdered, and pilgrims never stopped
w: Founded in 597 and rebuilt after a 1174 fire specifically to handle the pilgrims flocking to the shrine of Thomas Becket, the archbishop murdered here in 1170. It remains the mother church of the Anglican Communion and seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury - drawing pilgrims and the devout for eight centuries.
_facts: Founded in 597, completely rebuilt 1070-1077, Gothic east end after a 1174 fire
Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, was murdered here in 1170
Seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury and mother church of the Anglican Communion
Part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, receives around a million visitors a year

s: The abbey Henry VIII dismantled, piece by piece
w: Founded in 598 by Augustine of Canterbury himself, this Benedictine monastery survived nine centuries before the Reformation shut it in 1538 - after which it was stripped for stone until 1848. What remains stands as ruins beside the cathedral and St Martin's, together forming a single World Heritage Site.
_facts: Founded 598 as the Monastery of Ss Peter and Paul, renamed for Augustine of Canterbury
Benedictine monastery dissolved in 1538 during the English Reformation
Dismantled for building material until 1848, when part became used by The King's School
Forms a World Heritage Site together with Canterbury Cathedral and St Martin's Church

s: The 'Key to England' guarding the Channel crossing
w: Founded in the 11th century and nicknamed the 'Key to England' for commanding the shortest Channel crossing, this is sometimes claimed as the largest castle in the country - a title Windsor also fights for. Grade I listed, it still stands sentinel above the port that has watched every Channel departure since.
_facts: Medieval castle founded in the 11th century, Grade I listed
Nicknamed the 'Key to England' for its defensive significance
Sometimes described as the largest castle in England, a claim shared with Windsor Castle

s: An island castle Henry VIII gave to his first wife
w: A castle has stood on these lake islands since 857, but its golden age came under Edward I, who made it a favourite residence, and later Henry VIII, who housed his first wife Catherine of Aragon here. Its last private owner, Olive, Lady Baillie, left it in trust, and it has welcomed the public since 1976.
_facts: A castle has existed on the site since 857, built on islands in a lake on the River Len
Favourite residence of King Edward I in the 13th century
Henry VIII used it as a dwelling for his first wife, Catherine of Aragon
Last private owner Olive, Lady Baillie left it in trust; open to the public since 1976

s: The oldest church still in use in the English-speaking world
w: This modest parish church holds a startling claim: the oldest existing church in the English-speaking world, and the oldest English church building still in regular use for worship. It stands quietly beside Canterbury Cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey as the third leg of the city's World Heritage Site.
_facts: Oldest existing church in the English-speaking world
Oldest English church building still in ecclesiastical use
Part of the Canterbury World Heritage Site with the cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey
Part of the benefice of St Martin and St Paul Canterbury since 1668

s: Anne Boleyn's childhood home, later Henry's peace offering
w: Anne Boleyn spent her early years in this 13th-century moated house after her father inherited it in 1505 - a girlhood that ended with marriage to Henry VIII and her execution. Henry later gave the castle to his fourth wife, Anne of Cleves, as part of their divorce. Grade I listed, it still stands behind its moat.
_facts: Country house origins date to the 13th century
Seat of the Boleyn family from 1462 to 1539; Anne Boleyn grew up here from 1505
Later came into the possession of Henry VIII's fourth wife, Anne of Cleves
Grade I listed, now owned by the Guthrie family's Broadland Properties

s: England's second-oldest bishopric, rebuilt in Norman stone
w: Seat of the second-oldest bishopric in England, ranking behind only Canterbury, this Grade I listed cathedral was rebuilt in the Norman style on the footprint of its Anglo-Saxon predecessor. It has anchored the Diocese of Rochester for over a millennium, a quieter counterpart to its more famous neighbour up the road.
_facts: Seat of the Bishop of Rochester, the second-oldest bishopric in England after Canterbury
Formally the Cathedral Church of Christ and the Blessed Virgin Mary
Rebuilt on the site of its predecessor in the Norman style
Grade I listed building

s: An abbey built to atone for the Battle of Hastings
w: Built directly on the site of the Battle of Hastings and dedicated to St Martin of Tours, this Benedictine abbey has spent nearly a thousand years marking where 1066 changed English history. English Heritage now runs the ruins alongside the battlefield, with audio tours and a gatehouse displaying recovered artefacts.
_facts: Partially ruined Benedictine abbey built on the site of the Battle of Hastings
Dedicated to St Martin of Tours; now a Scheduled Monument and Grade I listed
Run by English Heritage as '1066 Battle of Hastings, Abbey and Battlefield'
Visitor centre includes a film, exhibition, and audio tours of the battlefield

s: A castle built as much to impress as to defend
w: Licensed by Richard II in 1385 against French invasion, Bodiam has no keep at all - just four towered corners and battlements around a wide moat, built to look as formidable as it functioned. It passed by marriage to the Lewknors, Lancastrian backers in the Wars of the Roses; a royal force besieged it in 1483.
_facts: 14th-century moated quadrangular castle built 1385 by Sir Edward Dalyngrigge
Licensed by Richard II ostensibly to defend against French invasion in the Hundred Years' War
Has no keep; chambers are built around the outer walls and towers, valuing display as much as defence
Passed to the Lewknor family, Lancastrian supporters besieged (unrecorded outcome) in 1483
